---
title: "Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)"
body-classes: fam-linear
---

[**Linear family**]{.fam-badge} · the supervised cousin of [PCA](pca.qmd): one model that does *both* classification and dimensionality reduction by projecting onto the directions that pull the classes apart. Siblings: [Logistic Regression](logistic.qmd) (also a linear classifier, but no dimensionality reduction and fewer distributional assumptions), QDA (one covariance *per* class), [PCA](pca.qmd) (unsupervised — variance, not class separation), [kNN](knn.qmd) (non-parametric alternative).

## 1. Essence

Linear Discriminant Analysis takes labelled data and finds the direction(s) along which the classes are most cleanly separated, then either reports a class for each point (classifier) or hands back the low-dimensional projection (dimensionality reduction). The guiding idea is a single trade-off, the **Fisher criterion**: choose the projection that makes the class *means* sit far apart (large **between-class** variance) while each class stays *tight* around its own mean (small **within-class** variance) (Lecture 3, slide 8/20; notebook `04_Linear_discriminant_analysis.ipynb`, cell 2). Because that projection is a linear combination of the features, the resulting decision boundary is a straight line (or hyperplane), and a $C$-class problem yields at most $C-1$ useful discriminant directions — which is why two classes collapse to a single axis.

It is a **parametric, generative** model: it assumes each class is drawn from a Gaussian and — crucially — that all classes **share one covariance matrix** (Lecture 3, slide 10/20). Under those assumptions LDA is the Bayes-optimal linear classifier; it trains in essentially one pass (estimate the class means, the pooled covariance, and the priors), needs little data, and gives an interpretable boundary. The shared-covariance assumption is exactly what makes the boundary *linear* — relax it (one covariance per class) and you get the quadratic boundary of QDA instead.

LDA wears two hats at once, which is its distinctive feature. As a **classifier** it competes with [logistic regression](logistic.qmd): both are linear, but LDA commits to the Gaussian/shared-covariance story while logistic regression models the log-odds directly and makes fewer distributional assumptions (Lecture 3, slide 11/20). As a **dimensionality reducer** it competes with [PCA](pca.qmd): PCA keeps the directions of greatest *total* variance ignoring labels, whereas LDA — being supervised — keeps the directions of greatest *class separation* (Lecture 3, slide 7/20).

## 2. When to use / when *not* to use

::: {.callout-intuition}
**Reach for LDA when…**

- The target is a **class** and you have **two or more reasonably well-separated classes** whose spreads (covariances) look **similar** (Lecture 3, slide 7/20).
- You want an **interpretable linear boundary** *and/or* a **supervised low-dimensional view** of the data — LDA gives you both from one fit. On Iris it compresses 4 features to 2 discriminants that visibly separate the three species (see §4).
- You want a **fast, low-variance baseline classifier** that needs little data — the model is just class means, a pooled covariance, and priors.
- You plan to **feed a downstream classifier** a cheaper representation: LDA is "frequently used as a preprocessing step before applying classifiers like logistic regression" (notebook `04_…`, cell 4).
:::

::: {.callout-pitfall}
**Reach for something else when…**

- **The classes have clearly different covariances (different shapes/orientations)** → the shared-covariance assumption is wrong and the linear boundary underfits. Use **QDA**, which estimates a separate covariance per class and gives a quadratic boundary (Lecture 3, slide 10/20).
- **You want minimal distributional assumptions for a linear classifier** → [**Logistic Regression**](logistic.qmd) models the log-odds directly without assuming Gaussian features; it is often the safer default when normality is doubtful (Lecture 3, slide 11/20).
- **You want dimensionality reduction but have no labels (or care about variance, not separation)** → [**PCA**](pca.qmd) is the unsupervised counterpart; LDA cannot run without `y` (it is supervised — "it requires the class labels to be passed … in the `fit` method", notebook `04_…`, cell 14).
- **The boundary is clearly non-linear** → [**kNN**](knn.qmd) or [**Decision Trees / Random Forests**](random_forests.qmd) drop the linear-form assumption (more flexible, less interpretable, hungrier for data).
:::

## 3. Code idiom

The canonical course idiom is `scikit-learn`'s `LinearDiscriminantAnalysis`; the course also builds LDA from scratch via the eigendecomposition of $S_W^{-1}S_B$ so the Fisher criterion is not a black box.

**Canonical (sklearn)** — *(notebook `04_Linear_discriminant_analysis.ipynb`, cell 8)*

```python
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis

# n_components: number of discriminant axes to keep after transform; must be ≤ #classes − 1
lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=1)   # 2-class toy data → at most 1 discriminant
lda.fit(X_train, y_train)                          # supervised: labels are REQUIRED
X_transformed = lda.transform(X_train)             # project onto the discriminant axis (dim reduction)
lda.predict(X_test)                                # class labels (classification)
lda.score(X_test, y_test)                          # mean accuracy
```

For multi-class dimensionality reduction the only change is `n_components` *(notebook `04_…`, cell 15)* — and `fit_transform` does fit-then-project in one call:

```python
lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=2)   # 3-class Iris → up to 2 discriminants (LD1, LD2)
X_train_lda = lda.fit_transform(X_train2, y_train2)  # fit on train, return its projection
X_test_lda  = lda.transform(X_test2)                 # project test with the SAME learned axes
```

The hyperparameters worth knowing (Lecture 3, slide 11/20): `solver` ∈ {`svd` (**default**, no covariance inversion, good for many features), `lsqr`, `eigen`}; `shrinkage` (regularizes the covariance estimate, only with `lsqr`/`eigen`); and `n_components` (the projection dimension, capped at #classes − 1). In notebook `04_…` everything except `n_components` is left at its `default`. Useful attributes: `coef_`, `means_`, `explained_variance_ratio_`. **Tip stressed in lecture:** scale/standardize features first (Lecture 3, slide 11/20; Lecture 4, slide 4/11).

**From scratch — eigendecomposition of $S_W^{-1}S_B$** *(notebook `04_…`, cell 18; this is the Tier-1 variation that fills the gap cell 4 leaves: "we will not dive into all the mathematical details")*. The heart of the class is: build the within- and between-class scatter, then take the eigenvectors of $\Sigma^{-1}S_B$:

```python
# within-class scatter S_W (sum of per-class outer products), then pooled covariance
S_W = np.zeros((n_features, n_features))
for c in self.classes_:
    X_c = X[y == c]; mean_c = self.means_[c].reshape(-1, 1)
    for x in X_c:
        x = x.reshape(-1, 1)
        S_W += (x - mean_c) @ (x - mean_c).T
self.cov_ = S_W / (n_samples - len(self.classes_))   # unbiased pooled cov, "consistent with sklearn"

# between-class scatter S_B = Σ_c N_c (μ_c − μ)(μ_c − μ)ᵀ
S_B = np.zeros((n_features, n_features))
for c in self.classes_:
    mean_diff = self.means_[c].reshape(-1, 1) - self.overall_mean_
    S_B += self.class_count_[c] * (mean_diff @ mean_diff.T)

# generalized eigenproblem: discriminant axes = top eigenvectors of inv(Σ) @ S_B
A = np.linalg.inv(self.cov_) @ S_B
eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eig(A)
idx = np.argsort(np.real(eigvals))[::-1]      # sort eigenvalues descending
self.W_ = np.real(eigvecs)[:, idx][:, :self.n_components]   # keep top n_components
```

::: {.callout-pitfall}
**Idiom variation worth knowing.** The from-scratch `predict` does **not** project-then-threshold; it applies the Gaussian/Bayes discriminant rule directly, $\delta_c(x) = x^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_c - \tfrac12\mu_c^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_c + \log\pi_c$, and takes the `argmax` over classes *(notebook `04_…`, cell 18)*. This is the same maximum-a-posteriori rule sklearn uses, which is why the two implementations agree to the digit on the toy set (see §4). If you ever quote the from-scratch test accuracy, recompute it — the notebook does not store that number (`phase0/disagreements.md` [NB-10]); the value below was computed in the venv.
:::

## 4. Worked examples

### Example 1 — toy 2-class set: classifier accuracy, sklearn vs from-scratch {#sec-lda-toy}

The course generates a 2-feature, 2-class toy set and fits LDA as a classifier *(notebook `04_…`, cell 6)*:

```python
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=200, n_features=2, n_redundant=0, n_informative=2,
                           n_clusters_per_class=1, class_sep=0.75, random_state=42)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.33, random_state=42)
LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=1).fit(X_train, y_train).score(X_test, y_test)
```

The stored notebook output is a **test accuracy of 0.7424** *(notebook `04_…`, cell 13, stored output `0.7424242424242424`)*. The modest score is the point, not a bug: `class_sep=0.75` makes the two Gaussians overlap substantially, so even the Bayes-optimal linear boundary cannot do much better — a vivid reminder that accuracy is bounded by how separable the classes actually are, not by the model's effort.

The from-scratch `LDAFromScratch(n_components=1)` *(cell 18–19)*, fit on the same split, reaches the **identical test accuracy of 0.7424** (train accuracy 0.7910 for both) — computed in the venv (`./.venv/Scripts/python.exe`, `random_state=42`), resolving the [VERIFY] flag in `phase0/disagreements.md` [NB-10]. The agreement is by design: both use the pooled (unbiased) covariance $S_W/(n-C)$ and the same Bayes discriminant rule, so they are *the same classifier*, just coded twice. The single non-trivial eigenvalue of $\Sigma^{-1}S_B$ is ≈ 77.4 (the second is numerically zero — there is only $C-1 = 1$ discriminant for two classes), computed in the venv.

::: {.callout-bigpicture}
This is the natural place to line LDA up against [**logistic regression**](logistic.qmd): on a 2-class problem both draw a straight boundary, but LDA *assumes* the two clouds are Gaussian with a shared covariance whereas logistic regression just fits the log-odds. When that assumption roughly holds (as here, by construction), they land in the same neighbourhood; when it fails badly, logistic regression usually degrades more gracefully. See the [2D classification showdown](../cross_method/showdowns.qmd).
:::

### Example 2 — Iris: LDA as supervised dimensionality reduction {#sec-lda-iris}

On Iris (150 samples, 4 features, 3 species) LDA wears its *other* hat — squashing 4 features to 2 discriminants for visualization *(notebook `04_…`, cell 15)*:

```python
iris = load_iris(); X2, y2 = iris.data, iris.target
X_train2, X_test2, y_train2, y_test2 = train_test_split(X2, y2, test_size=0.2, random_state=10)
lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=2)     # 3 classes → up to 2 discriminants
X_train_lda = lda.fit_transform(X_train2, y_train2)  # LD1, LD2 for the training set
X_test_lda  = lda.transform(X_test2)
```

The first discriminant carries almost everything: `explained_variance_ratio_ ≈ [0.992, 0.008]` — **LD1 alone accounts for ~99.2 % of the between-class separation** (computed in the venv, `random_state=10`). In the LD1–LD2 scatter the three species fall into cleanly separated bands, with *setosa* far from the other two. As a classifier on this split the same model scores **0.975 train / 1.00 test** accuracy (computed in the venv) — but with only 30 test points the perfect test score is small-sample luck, not a claim that Iris is trivially separable; report it as "high" rather than overreading the exact 1.00.

::: {.callout-bigpicture}
Contrast with [**PCA**](pca.qmd) on the *same* Iris data: PCA would pick the 2 directions of largest total variance **ignoring the species labels**, which need not be the directions that separate species. LDA's 99.2 %-on-LD1 result is precisely what supervision buys you — it spends its budget on *class* separation, not raw spread. This is the canonical "supervised vs unsupervised dimensionality reduction" comparison.
:::

Static prose can assert "LDA maximizes between-class over within-class variance"; only the picture shows the consequence — two clouds that LDA has pried apart as far as a single linear axis allows, with a stubborn overlap in the middle that caps accuracy at 0.74.

## 6. Diagnostics & interpretation

What to report and look at to decide whether an LDA model is working:

- **Accuracy / confusion matrix** — LDA is a classifier first; report test accuracy (toy: 0.74) and, for multi-class, the confusion matrix to see *which* classes get confused (Lecture 4, slide 4/11 explicitly recommends confusion matrices).
- **`explained_variance_ratio_`** — for the dimensionality-reduction hat, this tells you how much class separation each discriminant captures (Iris: LD1 ≈ 99.2 %). A first discriminant near 1.0 means a 1D view loses almost nothing.
- **Check the shared-covariance assumption** — if the classes visibly have different shapes/orientations, the linear boundary is mis-specified; that is the cue to move to **QDA**. Mild non-normality is usually tolerable ("robust to mild normality violations", Lecture 4, slide 4/11).
- **Did you standardize?** — scaling is stressed twice in lecture (L3 slide 11, L4 slide 4); on raw features with very different units the pooled covariance can be dominated by one feature.

::: {.callout-bigpicture}
Comparative diagnostic vs siblings: LDA gives you a *generative* story (class means + a shared covariance + priors), so you can read off how it would *generate* each class — where [logistic regression](logistic.qmd) gives only a *discriminative* boundary (the log-odds), and [PCA](pca.qmd) gives variance-ranked axes with no notion of class at all. Choose the model whose output answers your question: "which class, and why" (LDA), "what are the odds" (logistic), or "what varies most" (PCA).
:::

## 7. Past-exam lens

::: {.callout-exam}
**How LDA shows up.** LDA was **not examined in the Spring-2025 take-home** (`phase0/concept_inventory.md`; per rule R8 this absence is stated explicitly rather than glossed over) — the four assignments covered regression with regularization (Hitters), unsupervised PCA/K-means (WholesaleCustomers), trees/ensembles (WDBC), and a classifier comparison. LDA's most natural exam framing, *inferred* from how Lecture 3 teaches it, is comparative: (i) as a **2-class linear classifier set against [logistic regression](logistic.qmd)** — fit both, compare accuracy/boundaries, and discuss *which assumptions each makes* (LDA's Gaussian/shared-covariance vs logistic's distribution-free log-odds, Lecture 3 slide 11/20 gives the explicit comparison table); or (ii) as **supervised dimensionality reduction set against [PCA](pca.qmd)** — show that LDA's axes maximize *class* separation (Iris LD1 ≈ 99 %) while PCA's maximize total variance. If LDA appears, the marks would rest on *justifying the assumptions and the choice*, exactly as the regularization task rewards justifying shrinkage.
:::

## 8. Math {#sec-lda-math}

::: {.math-section}
::: {.math-off-hint}
*Math is off. Use the **Math** toggle in the top bar to show the course-level derivation (and "full" for the rigorous version).*
:::

::: {.callout-math-a}
**Mode A — course level.** The course frames LDA through **Fisher's criterion**: find the projection direction $w$ that pushes the class means apart while keeping each class tight *(notebook `04_Linear_discriminant_analysis.ipynb`, cell 2; Lecture 3, slide 8/20)*. Write the **between-class** and **within-class** scatter matrices
$$S_B = \sum_{i=1}^{C} N_i\,(m_i-m)(m_i-m)^\top, \qquad S_W = \sum_{i=1}^{C}\sum_{x\in C_i}(x-m_i)(x-m_i)^\top,$$
where $m_i = \tfrac{1}{N_i}\sum_{x\in C_i} x$ is the mean of class $i$ (size $N_i$) and $m$ is the overall mean *(slide 9/20)*. Fisher's criterion is the ratio of projected between- to within-class variance, which we maximize:
$$w = \arg\max_w \frac{w^\top S_B\, w}{w^\top S_W\, w}.$$
**Reading it:** the numerator $w^\top S_B w$ is how far apart the class means look *after* projecting onto $w$; the denominator $w^\top S_W w$ is how spread out each class looks along $w$ — so the ratio rewards separation and penalizes overlap. Setting the gradient of this ratio to zero turns it into a **generalized eigenproblem** whose top eigenvectors are the discriminant axes:
$$S_W^{-1}S_B\, w = \lambda w \qquad \text{(cell 3; slide 9/20).}$$
For **two classes** this collapses to a single closed form (only $C-1=1$ axis exists), and because $S_B$ then has rank one the direction is simply
$$w \propto S_W^{-1}(m_1-m_2) \qquad \text{(Lecture 3, slide 9/20)}$$
— the line joining the two means, "rotated" by $S_W^{-1}$ to undo the within-class spread. *Local notation note* (per `phase0/notation_table.md`): here $\lambda$ denotes an **LDA eigenvalue** (not a regularization strength), $m_i$ the class mean, $N_i$ the class size, and $w$ the **discriminant direction** (not a generic weight vector). See the [linear-algebra appendix](../appendix/math_appendix.qmd#sec-linalg).
:::

::: {.callout-math-b}
**Mode B — full rigor.** *(Anchored to ESL §4.3, eqs 4.7–4.12 and 4.15–4.16; verified at PDF pp. 126–135 = printed pp. 106–116.)* ESL derives LDA from **decision theory**, not from Fisher's ratio. Let $f_k(x)$ be the class-conditional density and $\pi_k$ the prior of class $k$ (with $\sum_k\pi_k=1$). Bayes' theorem gives the posterior
$$\Pr(G=k\mid X=x) = \frac{f_k(x)\,\pi_k}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K f_\ell(x)\,\pi_\ell} \qquad \text{(ESL 4.7),}$$
so classifying to the largest posterior is **Bayes-optimal**. Now model each class as a multivariate Gaussian
$$f_k(x) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{p/2}\lvert\Sigma_k\rvert^{1/2}}\,\exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac12 (x-\mu_k)^\top\Sigma_k^{-1}(x-\mu_k)\Bigr) \qquad \text{(ESL 4.8).}$$
**LDA is the special case of a shared covariance** $\Sigma_k=\Sigma\ \forall k$. Comparing two classes by their log-posterior ratio,
$$\log\frac{\Pr(G=k\mid x)}{\Pr(G=\ell\mid x)} = \log\frac{\pi_k}{\pi_\ell} - \tfrac12(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell) + x^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell) \qquad \text{(ESL 4.9),}$$
which is **linear in $x$**: the shared $\Sigma$ makes the normalizing constants *and* the quadratic term $x^\top\Sigma^{-1}x$ cancel between the two classes. The boundary $\{x:\Pr(G=k\mid x)=\Pr(G=\ell\mid x)\}$ is therefore a hyperplane. Equivalently, classify by $G(x)=\arg\max_k \delta_k(x)$ using the **linear discriminant functions**
$$\delta_k(x) = x^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k - \tfrac12\mu_k^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k + \log\pi_k \qquad \text{(ESL 4.10)}$$
— *exactly* the rule the from-scratch `predict` implements *(notebook `04_…`, cell 18)*, with the plug-in estimates $\hat\pi_k=N_k/N$, $\hat\mu_k=\sum_{g_i=k}x_i/N_k$, and the **pooled** covariance $\hat\Sigma=\sum_{k}\sum_{g_i=k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^\top/(N-K)$ (the $N-K$ denominator is why the notebook's `S_W/(n−C)` "matches sklearn"). **Why this matters: QDA.** If the $\Sigma_k$ are *not* assumed equal, the quadratic term survives and you get the quadratic discriminant $\delta_k(x)=-\tfrac12\log\lvert\Sigma_k\rvert-\tfrac12(x-\mu_k)^\top\Sigma_k^{-1}(x-\mu_k)+\log\pi_k$ (ESL 4.12) — a curved boundary. Shared covariance ⇔ linear; per-class covariance ⇔ quadratic.

**Equivalence to Fisher's criterion.** ESL §4.3.3 shows the Mode-A view is the *same* model. Writing $B$ for the between-class covariance of the centroids and $W$ for the within-class (pooled) covariance, Fisher's "maximize between- over within-class variance" is the **Rayleigh quotient**
$$\max_a \frac{a^\top B\, a}{a^\top W\, a} \qquad \text{(ESL 4.15)} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \max_a a^\top B\, a \ \text{ s.t. } a^\top W a = 1 \qquad \text{(ESL 4.16),}$$
"a generalized eigenvalue problem, with $a$ given by the largest eigenvalue of $W^{-1}B$" — identical in form to Mode A's $S_W^{-1}S_B w=\lambda w$ ($B,W$ are ESL's names for $S_B,S_W$, and $B+W=T$, the total covariance). ESL notes Fisher "arrived at this decomposition via a different route, without referring to Gaussian distributions at all," yet it lands on the same discriminant directions — the two derivations agree (`phase0/disagreements.md`: LDA Fisher criterion and $w\propto S_W^{-1}(m_1-m_2)$ match ESL §4.3; no flags). One subtlety ESL flags: the least-squares/Fisher route fixes the *direction* but the Gaussian route is needed to set the *intercept* (cut-point) — for two classes the two agree only when $N_1=N_2$ (ESL eq. 4.11 and following). See the [linear-algebra appendix](../appendix/math_appendix.qmd#sec-linalg).
